abstract: Recent efforts to discover new protein-coding genes in the human genome have yielded a large number of short open reading frames supported by limited experimental evidence supporting translational activity in fragmented parts of those sequences. We examined the 19 highest-confidence predictions made by the TransCODE Consortium, and found that three of them were previously known and thus not novel, while the other 16 could be explained by mechanisms that do not require the assertion of a novel human protein. In several cases, the alternative explanations for the other 16 had already been published. We also analyzed the other 118 predictions and found that most of these, too, could be explained without positing the existence of novel proteins. Our findings show that in the search for new human genes, evidence of transcription and translation can almost always be explained by known mechanisms, and that the predictions of the TransCODE Consortium likely do not include any novel genes.
